items.claim: Nmap service version detection with -sV probes open ports to identify the running service and its version.
items.body: Running nmap -sV against a target sends service-specific probes to open ports and matches responses against a signature database. Increasing --version-intensity to 9 sends more probes, identifying services that disguise themselves or run on non-standard ports. Version data feeds vulnerability research and patch-level assessment.
items.disproof: Ports are filtered or closed, or version detection returns no match for any service.

sources.quote: Service Enumeration | Identifying services, versions, and banner grabbing
Service enumeration is the stage where I stop guessing what is behind a port

items.claim: Banner grabbing connects to a service and reads its initial response, revealing service name, version, and OS hints.
items.body: Many services send a banner on connection. Nmap captures banners automatically with -sV --script=banner. Manual grabbing uses nc to connect to a port and read the response. Banners often leak version strings and configuration details useful for fingerprinting and vulnerability matching.
items.disproof: The service sends no banner, or banners are stripped by a reverse proxy or load balancer.

sources.quote: Banner grabbing is essential to identify detailed information about the services

items.claim: A full port scan with nmap -p- -sV identifies all 65535 ports and the services running on each, providing complete attack surface visibility.
items.body: Scanning all ports with -p- followed by -sV ensures no service on a non-standard port is missed. Verbose mode (-v) shows open ports as they are found, allowing real-time analysis. This is slower but necessary for thorough internal reconnaissance.
items.disproof: All 65535 ports are filtered by a firewall, or scan time constraints prevent full coverage.
